title: Unit Planning
author: Dylan Kane
summary: Dylan Kane argues that the heart of effective lesson planning is not the individual lesson but the unit -- a three-to-seven-week stretch of instruction -- and describes the three goals he pursues at that level: coherence, practice, and engagement. He relies on the Illustrative Math curriculum for coherence, crediting its sequencing, representations, and rigor with saving him the work of building that structure himself, while treating practice as the piece any packaged curriculum handles worst and therefore something he must build in himself based on what he sees students need. Kane walks through his actual planning process: writing every lesson, activity, and practice idea on slips of paper, arranging them into a flow that shows how one lesson sets up the next, then paring the resulting sprawl down to what's manageable. He is careful to frame this as building on top of a high-quality curriculum rather than replacing it, arguing that neither teaching with no curriculum nor following one with rigid fidelity serves students well. Kane closes by defending planning even a rough unit outline in advance, including deliberately built-in slack for disruptions, against the view that planning more than a day or two ahead is pointless.
points: Kane's three unit-planning goals -- coherence, practice, and engagement -- map onto three different sources: the packaged curriculum (coherence), the teacher's own judgment (practice), and deliberate substitution of stale packaged tasks (engagement).

His physical planning method -- slips of paper for every lesson, activity, and practice idea, arranged into a visual flow -- takes about an hour, eight times a year, which he calls the most valuable planning time he spends.

Kane pushes back on two extremes: teaching with no curriculum at all (unsustainable for new teachers) and following a curriculum with rigid fidelity (which ignores whether students are actually learning).

He deliberately builds two to three weeks of slack into his yearly schedule for lockdowns, weather, and other disruptions, arguing that unit-level planning without any rough outline is "irresponsible."
quotes: I've found that the heart of planning is much more about the unit than the lesson.
The structure and sequencing of the units, the thoughtful use of representations, the variety of contexts and word problems, and the level of rigor save me tons of work trying to do all that myself.
I end up with a giant list of everything I could possible include, and then pare it down to what is manageable and focused on my biggest priorities.

Plenty of teachers can teach well without any curriculum, but it’s not sustainable for new teachers and inventing your own curriculum takes valuable time away from all the other things teachers need to do.
I also think going into a unit without at least a rough plan is irresponsible.
